body:
Today's scan turned up two flagged arbitrage pairs, and both are the kind of near-nothing you'd expect on a normal day rather than free money. The larger one pairs a Polymarket contract on gold touching a $4,700 high in August (yes at 7.9¢) against a Kalshi contract settling above $4,731.99 on August 31 (no at 91¢). The combined cost is 98.9¢ against a $1 payout, but after fees the net edge is only about half a cent per contract, and the book only supports 47 contracts — roughly 25 cents of total profit. That gap exists mainly because the two contracts aren't measuring the same thing: Polymarket pays out if gold ever touches $4,700 intraday during August, while Kalshi pays based on the settlement price at 5pm ET on August 31 against a different strike ($4,731.99). A touch-anytime contract and an end-of-month settle contract with different thresholds will price differently even with no real dislocation.

The second pair is entirely within Polymarket — a ladder between two "touch low" contracts ($4,150 and $4,100) for the week of August 17. It's logically airtight (hitting the lower strike guarantees the higher one was also hit), but the mispricing is a tenth of a cent, capped at about ten contracts, for a whole cent of profit. That's noise-level, not tradeable.

Context for why so many strikes sit near $4,300–$4,700: gold has been rallying hard. It traded near $4,070 on August 4 and had jumped to a $4,400 open by August 10. Gold (GC=F) December futures opened at $4,400 per troy ounce on Monday, August 10, 2026, flat compared to Friday's closing price, following a rise that had already pushed prices to $4,411.70 at 8:45 a.m. ET on August 7 amid a weak jobs report. Both platforms' contract ladders are simply repricing quickly around that move, which is the more plausible explanation than a genuine cross-platform edge.
headline: Two flagged gold arbitrage pairs are noise, not free money
